Baby & Child

When your child cannot pass a hard stool

Updated: October 7, 2026

Written and edited byMohammadamin Namyar, founder of BeMama: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

A stool that seems stuck can distress both a child and a parent. The safest response depends on the child’s age, pain and other symptoms: not simply on how long it has been since the last bowel movement.

A hard stool can hurt even without a bowel obstruction

A child who seems to have a stool stuck at the anus may be frightened as well as uncomfortable. Hard, dry stool can be difficult to pass, particularly after a previous painful bowel movement. Constipation is common, but a child who is very unwell or has severe pain needs assessment rather than repeated attempts to push.

Constipation is more than a count of toilet visits. Painful passage, hard pellets, unusually large stools, withholding and a feeling of incomplete emptying can matter even if some stool passes every day. A universal fewer-than-three-times-a-week rule is not suitable for every age, especially for breastfed babies.

Faecal impaction and overflow are different from ordinary diarrhoea

Faecal impaction means a build-up of retained stool that needs to be cleared. It can follow prolonged constipation and withholding. A child may have bloating, reduced appetite, discomfort or repeated small amounts of stool without adequately emptying the bowel.

Loose stool can seep around the retained mass and soil underwear. This overflow can look like diarrhoea even though constipation is the underlying problem. The child may not feel it happening. Scolding, treating the child as deliberately dirty or giving diarrhoea medicine without assessment can make the situation harder.

Impaction should be assessed and treated, but it is not identical to a complete intestinal obstruction. Nor can its presence be decided merely because one stool is large or appears stuck at the opening. The history and an appropriate examination guide the diagnosis.

Why the pain-and-withholding cycle develops

After a hard stool hurts, a child may try to avoid the next one. They might stiffen, stand on tiptoes, clench their bottom, cross their legs or hide. What looks like straining to pass stool can actually be an effort to hold it in. Stool retained longer loses more water and becomes harder to pass.

Toilet-training pressure, unfamiliar school toilets, lack of privacy, anxiety or not wanting to interrupt play can all contribute. The problem is not solved simply by telling a child to try harder. They need comfortable stools and a routine that feels safe enough to use.

Diet, fluids, activity and medicines can contribute

Low fibre intake or insufficient fluid can contribute to hard stools. A varied diet containing fruit, vegetables, beans and whole grains supports bowel health. Ordinary age-appropriate activity is useful too, but most children’s constipation cannot be explained simply by sitting down too much.

Some medicines and supplements can worsen constipation, including iron, certain seizure medicines and some pain medicines. Tell the clinician what the child takes, including products bought without a prescription. Do not stop an important medicine yourself; an adjustment may be possible if it is contributing.

Food and routine changes support treatment, but established impaction usually needs more than extra fruit or water. Adding large amounts of fibre or fibre supplements without an appropriate plan can increase discomfort and does not reliably clear a retained stool mass.

Babies need a separate approach

Starting solids or changing feeds can change stool consistency. This is not a bodily shock that parents should simply wait out if stools become hard and painful. Offer suitable foods for the baby’s stage and discuss persistent difficulty with a health professional.

Some young babies strain, grunt or turn red before passing a soft stool because they are still coordinating the muscles involved. Soft stool and otherwise normal feeding and growth are different from hard-stool constipation. A breastfed baby’s stool frequency can also vary considerably.

Prepare formula exactly as directed; extra powder can cause dehydration and harder stools. Do not dilute feeds or give a young infant water, juice, laxatives or rectal treatments without appropriate advice. Contact the baby’s clinician promptly for feeding difficulties, hard stools or an unexplained change, particularly in the early weeks.

Sometimes an underlying condition needs investigation

Most childhood constipation is functional, meaning it is not explained by an underlying structural disease. A smaller group of children need investigation for conditions such as Hirschsprung disease, coeliac disease, hypothyroidism or disorders affecting the brain, spinal cord or nerves. A history of surgery or neurological injury may also be relevant.

Constipation from birth, delayed passage of the first meconium, poor growth, persistent abdominal swelling or new leg or bladder difficulties deserves particular attention. Do not wait for a routine dietary trial when a newborn has not passed the first stool or seems unwell.

Irritable bowel syndrome and inflammatory bowel conditions require their own assessment and are not interchangeable with a retained hard stool. Parkinson’s disease, colorectal cancer and anal cancer can appear in adult constipation discussions, but they should not be presented as usual causes in children. The child’s age and clinical findings determine which rare explanations warrant investigation.

What to do when a stool will not come out

Pause the struggle and reassure the child. For a toilet-trained child who is otherwise comfortable, offer a secure seat with feet supported and allow a short, unhurried attempt. If nothing happens, stop rather than demanding prolonged straining. Gentle movement or a comfortably warm bath may help comfort, but cannot guarantee that impaction will clear.

If a stool appears stuck and the child remains in pain or cannot pass it, contact a clinician for timely advice. Describe the child’s age, last comfortable bowel movement, stool consistency, any soiling and whether there is vomiting, swelling, fever or bleeding. Follow an existing constipation plan if one has been prescribed, and ask for advice if it is not working.

Avoid pulling, probing and repeated unsupervised treatments

Do not pull stool out with your fingers, insert objects or attempt to break it apart. The anal lining can tear and bleed, and an invasive attempt can increase fear and withholding. Manual evacuation, when exceptionally needed, is a clinical procedure rather than a home remedy.

Do not give an adult enema or combine several laxative products because the first attempt has not worked. Suppositories and enemas have specific indications, age restrictions and risks. Sodium phosphate preparations can cause serious dehydration and electrolyte disturbances, with kidney or heart injury; their rectal form must not be used in children under two.

A medicine being available over the counter does not make it suitable for every child. Ask for the correct product and instructions, and seek help instead of repeatedly increasing a dose.

Know when this needs urgent or emergency care

Seek urgent medical assessment for persistent or severe abdominal pain, significant swelling, repeated vomiting, blood in the stool, fever with illness, dehydration or weight loss. Green vomit, a very swollen painful abdomen or inability to pass gas with vomiting can indicate obstruction and requires emergency assessment.

Call emergency services if the child collapses, becomes confused, is difficult to wake, has breathing difficulty or appears severely unwell. A racing heartbeat, marked weakness or very little urine can accompany significant illness or dehydration. Do not rely on a constipation diagnosis to explain away these changes.

An isolated headache or a particular stool shape cannot diagnose obstruction. Conversely, you do not need every warning sign before seeking help. If you are concerned about a baby or a rapidly worsening child, obtain urgent advice.

How a clinician assesses and clears a stool build-up

Assessment begins with the history, growth and an appropriate examination. The clinician will ask about pain, withholding, stool leakage, medicines and symptoms from infancy. Rectal examination is not a task for a parent and is not required in every child.

For diagnosed functional impaction, an oral macrogol or polyethylene glycol, often called PEG, is commonly first-line. The formulation and regimen depend on age and local practice. A clinician may adjust treatment or add another laxative if needed. Clearing the build-up can temporarily increase soiling or cramping; arrange follow-up and report significant deterioration.

NICE advises review within a week during disimpaction. Rectal medicines are generally reserved for situations in which an appropriate oral regimen has failed and should involve consent and professional direction. Do not assume that a suppository or enema is the first or safest step.

Colonoscopy, routine scans and surgery are not usual investigations or treatments for uncomplicated functional constipation. Persistent problems or alarm features can justify specialist tests. A true obstruction requires its own urgent management rather than simply a stronger home laxative.

Treatment often continues after the first comfortable stool

Clearing retained stool is only the first stage. A maintenance plan keeps new stools soft while the bowel and the child’s confidence recover. Stopping after one large bowel movement can allow the pain-and-withholding cycle to begin again.

There is no blanket rule that a child’s prescribed laxative must stop after two weeks. Treatment often continues for months, with review and gradual reduction when symptoms are consistently controlled. Some children need longer support, particularly through toilet training. The prescriber should explain the plan and when to make contact.

Track comfort, stool consistency, leakage and how the child manages toileting, not just whether a stool appeared that day. If medicine is difficult to take, discuss the practical problem openly so the regimen can be adjusted.

Prevent recurrence with a routine the child can manage

Build brief toilet opportunities into the day, often after meals, and provide a footstool or suitable potty. Praise cooperation and sitting comfortably rather than rewarding only the production of a stool. Respond to the urge to go instead of postponing it until after an activity.

Offer a variety of age-appropriate fibre-containing foods and usual fluids. Avoid turning eating into a battle or making a child drink excessive amounts. If appetite or food variety is very restricted, ask for help developing a realistic plan.

Check whether school or childcare toilets feel safe, clean and accessible. A private conversation with staff about timely toilet access and spare clothes may make treatment easier. Accidental soiling should be handled calmly; it is a symptom to address, not a behaviour to punish.

Complications are a reason for early help, not panic

Painful hard stools can cause an anal fissure, a small tear that may leave bright blood on wiping. Ongoing retention can cause persistent soiling and discomfort. Haemorrhoids or rectal prolapse may occur in some circumstances and need assessment rather than a parent assuming the diagnosis.

Severe untreated obstruction is a different and potentially dangerous situation. It can compromise bowel blood supply or lead to inflammation or infection of the abdominal lining, called peritonitis. Rare pressure-related tissue injury can occur with severe stool retention. These are not the expected consequences of an ordinary episode of childhood constipation.

Low blood pressure, collapse, confusion, fever or a rapidly worsening condition calls for emergency assessment. Seeking help early for painful stools and following a maintenance plan reduces the chance of a prolonged problem.

A separate note for a pregnant parent with constipation

Pregnancy-related hormonal changes can slow bowel movement; lower activity, dietary changes and iron supplements may contribute too. This adult context needs its own advice and should not be used to select a child’s medicine or dose.

A pregnant person can discuss suitable food, fluid, activity and medication options with the maternity team or pharmacist. Do not stop prescribed iron without advice. Severe pain, persistent vomiting, marked distension or suspected obstruction requires prompt assessment rather than continued self-treatment.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Hard or painful stools and withholding matter alongside frequency; overflow can look like diarrhoea.

Treatment may require supervised disimpaction followed by sustained maintenance.

Adult constipation treatments and age-independent laxative rules should not be applied to children.

How BeMama can help

Keep the response calm, record symptoms and use a written treatment and follow-up plan with the child’s clinician.

When to seek help

Severe pain, a swollen abdomen, green or repeated vomiting, collapse or a very unwell child needs urgent assessment. Do not manually remove stool or use unsupervised enemas.

Evidence notes updated: October 7, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Some daily stool or leakage does not rule out constipation.
  • Withholding often follows pain and needs practical support.
  • A baby’s feeding and stool pattern require age-specific assessment.
  • Prescribed treatment may need to continue for months.
  • Emergency symptoms should not be attributed to simple constipation.

Frequently asked questions

Does a daily bowel movement rule out constipation?

No. A child may pass small hard stools or overflow around a retained mass. Comfort, consistency, withholding and whether the bowel is emptying adequately matter as well as frequency.

Is runny stool in underwear always diarrhoea?

No. Overflow can leak around retained hard stool, sometimes without the child noticing. Seek assessment before assuming the child needs diarrhoea treatment.

Should I pull out a stool that is visible at the opening?

No. Pulling or probing can damage tissue and increase pain and fear. If the child cannot pass it or remains distressed, contact a clinician for appropriate help.

Can extra fibre and water clear an impaction?

They support normal bowel health but do not reliably clear an established build-up by themselves. A clinician may prescribe a disimpaction regimen followed by maintenance treatment.

Can I use an adult enema for my child?

Do not use it without specific clinical direction. Products differ, and sodium phosphate enemas in particular can cause serious harm and must not be given to children under two.

Must prescribed laxatives stop after two weeks?

No. There is no blanket two-week limit for a supervised childhood constipation plan. Treatment often continues for months and is reduced gradually when symptoms are controlled, with review.

Does a baby straining always need a laxative?

No. Straining before a soft stool can reflect developing coordination. Hard stools, poor feeding, illness or a concerning change need age-specific assessment rather than an automatic laxative.

When should I seek emergency care?

Get urgent help for green vomit, severe or persistent pain, a markedly swollen abdomen or inability to pass gas with vomiting. Collapse, difficulty waking or a severely unwell child requires emergency services.

Will my child need a colonoscopy or surgery?

These are not routine for functional constipation. Alarm features, persistent problems or suspected underlying disease may lead to specialist investigation; true obstruction has a separate urgent pathway.

How can I reduce fear of the toilet?

Offer a stable seat and supported feet, short relaxed opportunities and praise for trying. Address privacy or school-toilet concerns, and keep stools comfortable through the agreed treatment plan.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
